name: Tomas Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First I check which shops need power off before opening time, then I split the jobs with the other electrician. I'm 27, with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I lead the awkward fault calls. My partner Mira and I rent a small flat, with no children and only eighteen days of expenses saved. The pay is low despite the responsibility, there are few nearby employers, and I sometimes use AI to tidy an appointment email after a colleague showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a relief, and ask whether the repair van is finally getting its broken shelf fixed. I don't mind a useful phone tool, but the van is where the tools fall on my feet. A quiet change would suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't lose sleep over AI in that picture. I'd still worry about the rent, because I earn less than other electricians despite leading jobs. I've got eighteen days of expenses saved, so being good at work doesn't make a missed week harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on with the shop and house repairs. Starting this week I'll check the van stock before ordering so I don't pay for emergency bits myself and wait for reimbursement. For the first year I'll set aside 15 from each weekly wage until I have a month's expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a familiar sort of worry, the one I carry when the bank message arrives. The work itself feels solid. I can do something about the little cash leaks without making a grand announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are you paying for parts yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes the nearest supplier won't put a small purchase on the firm's account. I pay to finish the job, then the receipt sits in a tray for a week. I'll ask the owner to keep the common parts stocked instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does AI fit into your work today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've occasionally used a tool to tidy an email about an appointment, after a colleague showed me. I don't use it to decide whether a circuit is safe. My tester and my own checks do that.

say: I'd welcome **quiet change** and ask for the repair van's broken shelf to be fixed.
I'd rather improve **daily equipment** than make a fuss over a useful phone tool.
think: I don't fear **AI** here, but low pay makes the rent difficult despite leading jobs.
My **eighteen-day cushion** means a missed working week would still cause trouble at home.
do: Keep doing **house and shop repairs** through the first year.
Check **van stock** now to avoid paying for emergency parts while awaiting reimbursement.
Save **15 weekly** from wages until a month's expenses are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary income interruptions, with confidence in the repair work itself.
S0.quote: I've got eighteen days of expenses saved, so being good at work doesn't make a missed week harmless.
fieldNote: His **cash pressure** includes personally funded parts awaiting reimbursement, making ordinary business routines matter alongside wages and savings.
He uses **AI occasionally** for appointment emails after a colleague's example, while retaining physical testing and safety decisions himself.

steps.text: Keep completing house and shop electrical repairs
Save 15 from each weekly wage until one month is covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner that quicker quotes could be useful if somebody checks what's been left out. An old shop isn't a blank room with straight walls. I'd give a tool a chance after seeing it work on jobs we already understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booking and quote work will change before pulling cables does. I'm worried the owner might promise cheaper repairs and expect us to make the difference in speed. My hours or pay could get squeezed even if nobody has a robot in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my colleague Niko to show me the quoting tool on one completed job this month, with the owner's permission. If the comparison held up, I'd practise on two more completed jobs before using a draft on live work. In the first year I'd check every quoted materials list myself and keep saving the 15 a week while my wage allows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm watchful, not excited. Seeing a real comparison would calm me more than watching an advert. I don't want to be the electrician who rejects a useful tool, or the one who sends a customer a confident mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the comparison fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool left out isolating the supply or assumed we could reach a cable without opening a wall, I'd stop there. I'd show Niko the missing item and keep using our checked method. The owner needs a believable price, not just a quick one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your savings if hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and food come before the 15. I'd reduce the deposit if I had to, rather than borrow money to claim I was saving. I'm not counting extra pay from the quoting tool because nobody has offered any.

say: I'd give a **quoting tool** a chance after seeing it handle familiar completed jobs correctly.
I'd insist that faster **quotes** still include awkward access and proper safety work.
think: I worry **cheaper quotes** could become pressure to finish physical repairs faster.
My **pay or hours** could shrink before any robot arrives to pull cables.
do: Ask my **colleague** to demonstrate a quoting tool on completed jobs with the owner's permission.
Check each **materials list** myself if the tool proves useful during the first year.
Continue saving **15 weekly** only while wages cover rent and food.
feel: **Anxious** about earnings, while willing to judge a tool from checked examples.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the electrician who rejects a useful tool, or the one who sends a customer a confident mistake.
fieldNote: His **steady adaptability** involves permission, demonstration and repeated checks rather than immediate adoption or a refusal to learn.
The **saving condition** is explicit: household essentials come first, and he does not assume software creates a wage increase.

steps.text: Practise AI quoting on completed jobs if the owner permits a checked trial
Save 15 weekly while wages still cover rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that electrical repairs don't become desk work in 2028. I'd also say the breathing space ends around 2031 when the robots can do hands-on work. I wouldn't use the first date to sell false comfort about the second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm scared our ordinary installation work could earn much less once the robots arrive. There are few similar employers nearby, and all might be facing the same change. I can picture losing a big part of my income just as I've finally got the licence and the responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd cancel the weekend meals out and put that 30 a week towards the cash cushion while I'm earning. I'd ask two nearby repair firms this month about their actual vacancies, without giving up this job. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for an advertised fault-repair post only if the pay and paid hours covered our rent and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, because two years is short when the starting balance is so low. Looking for work gives me something to do, but I know another firm isn't outside the same world. I don't want my partner carrying all the fear silently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say over dinner to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner, Mira, that we should stop booking restaurant tables for a while and look at the rent together. My partner works in a plant nursery, but I wouldn't assume those wages can carry both of us. I'd bring the actual numbers, not just a gloomy video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a fault-repair post worth considering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A listed wage isn't enough if the employer won't promise paid hours. I'd ask about the minimum hours, the travel and whether tools were provided. I won't hand in notice because somebody says there might be work.

say: I'd tell my **partner** repairs remain physical in 2028, with capable robots following around 2031.
I wouldn't call the **three-year gap** permanent protection for electrical work.
think: I expect **installation income** could fall sharply once robots can do the physical work.
Few **nearby employers** limit my options, and other firms may face the same change.
do: Cancel **restaurant meals** now and save the 30 weekly while earning.
Ask two **repair firms** about actual vacancies this month without leaving my current job.
Apply after **2028** only for advertised repair posts whose paid hours cover rent and travel.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing a large share of income, with job searches offering limited control.
S2.quote: I won't hand in notice because somebody says there might be work.
fieldNote: He expects a major **later income loss**, but his first-year response after 2028 remains a conditional search for physical repair work.
The **job change** depends on a posted vacancy, adequate pay and paid hours; his partner's income is not assumed sufficient.

steps.text: Save the 30 weekly restaurant budget while still earning
Apply after 2028 for posted repair jobs with adequate pay and paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me time to add a skill deliberately, instead of running at the nearest course. I still want to earn through my trade. Thinking systems arriving in 2031 and robots around 2034 means I have to check what a course would actually teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have a better cash buffer before the office side changes, and that matters. I'd still worry about my hours because better qualifications don't make demand appear. I want a useful second string within repair work, not a certificate that promises I'm beyond machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the owner to fund a short course on finding faults in older building controls, the switches and wiring that run heating and lighting. I'd enrol only if the fees were covered and the class time was paid; I can't stop earning. In the first year after 2031 I'd ask for those repair calls and keep a record of whether the extra training actually protected my paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but more purposeful than in the two-year picture. Five years lets me test an option while still earning. I wouldn't call the course a rescue until I'd checked both the funding and the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner refuses to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't enrol on credit. I'd keep working and build the cash cushion from the meals I cut, provided earnings still covered essentials. A course that makes me miss rent isn't a sensible plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why older building controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already get calls where the lighting timer talks to an old heating switch and nobody knows which cable matters. I can trace faults well, but I'd like formal teaching on those linked systems. I'm not claiming robots will never manage them; I'd be buying time to earn, if the course really fits our calls.

say: I'd use **five years** to choose useful teaching rather than rush into the nearest course.
I want to keep earning through **repair work**, with honest checks on what training can deliver.
think: A larger **cash buffer** before 2031 would make change less frightening than the two-year timetable.
Extra **qualifications** cannot guarantee enough demand or protect my hours from machines.
do: Request **employer funding** now for a course on faults in older heating and lighting controls.
Enrol only with **fees covered** and paid class time, continuing savings if funding is refused.
Seek **controls repair calls** after 2031 and record whether training protects paid hours.
feel: **Anxious**, but more purposeful because an option can be tested without assuming lost wages are affordable.
S3.quote: A course that makes me miss rent isn't a sensible plan.
fieldNote: His **training proposal** builds on current fault-finding skill and observed calls, rather than inventing an entirely new occupation.
Enrolment remains conditional on **covered fees** and paid class time; qualification gains are not treated as immunity from capable robots.

steps.text: Enrol in controls fault training only with employer-paid fees and paid class time
Continue saving the meal budget if funding is refused and essentials remain covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets us plan more than the next bill, if we use it. I'd rather learn changes as a working electrician than wait nine years and complain. I'd still check each new tool on a real job before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 leaves time to build experience, but I'd only be 37 then, not finished working. I think repair demand would hold over the next few years, though a missed week would still threaten our rent with this little saved. Robots around 2039 could reach the tasks I rely on, so I want cash and choices before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving 15 weekly now and request the funded controls course, with the same paid-time condition. I'd review the plan with my partner every six months rather than sign for a larger flat. In the first year after 2036 I'd continue paid controls and wiring repairs while checking whether hours still covered essentials before spending on further training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still anxious about a missed working week, but the distant AI date doesn't add the same rush. The long date makes the next few years look manageable, not the rest of my life guaranteed. I'd like to look back and see I used some of that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on the table at the six-month review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings balance, our rent and the number of paid hours from the previous month. My partner and I have no children and aren't trying to plan every future choice today. We'd keep our present flat while the cushion is this thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the longer date change your view of asking for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still ask the owner to support training, because better work is useful to the firm too. I prefer earning my way and getting useful teaching to assuming a payment will appear later. If I needed family help I'd ask honestly, but I haven't built a family payment into this plan.

say: I'd use the **decade** to learn changes while earning rather than leave everything until the last year.
I'd still test **new tools** on familiar work before trusting their output.
think: I expect **repair demand** to hold, but a missed week could still threaten our rent with so little saved.
I'll be only **37** in 2036, so later robots still matter to my working life.
do: Save **15 weekly** now and seek the controls course only with funded fees and paid time.
Review **rent and savings** with my partner every six months before considering a larger flat.
Continue **paid repairs** after 2036 and check hours before purchasing further training.
feel: **Anxious** about a missed week's pay, with less urgency around distant automation.
S4.quote: The long date makes the next few years look manageable, not the rest of my life guaranteed.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** reduces the added automation rush while his present savings and income-interruption worries remain explicit.
His **household review** uses actual rent, hours and savings; training support is requested from the employer without assumed future family payments.

steps.text: Take controls course only with funded fees and paid class time
Keep paid controls and wiring repairs after 2036 while checking actual hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the robots following around 2031 could cut a big part of my earnings before I've built a buffer. Employer-paid training with paid class time would help, plus repair vacancies that state real paid hours. I want a way to keep earning, not a course bill I can't carry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how long people wait to get their own money back after buying parts for work. My toolbox shouldn't be lending money to my employer while my rent is due. That little delay matters when your savings don't cover a month.

headlineQuote: My toolbox shouldn't be lending money to my employer while my rent is due.
portrait: Tomas is **27**, a highly skilled licensed repair lead with a technical diploma, low pay and fewer than three weeks' expenses saved.
He rents with his **partner**, has no children, and occasionally uses AI for emails after seeing a colleague demonstrate it.
He responds to short deadlines with **spending cuts** and conditional job applications, insisting on actual vacancies and adequate paid hours.
Longer timetables allow **funded training** and household reviews, with no assumption that qualifications defeat robots or retirement is close.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little buffer-building time before robots could sharply reduce his earnings around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Employer-funded training** with paid class time would let him learn without losing essential income.
Repair vacancies stating **paid hours** would make job searches more useful than vague promises of work.
